title: Decompose request aggregator and compact key-value store sync
creator: Ava Patel
description:
Background:
The current request aggregator is a large, single-stage component that co-ordinates continuous batching, slot allocation, and the KV prefix store synchronization. Over time it has accumulated locking paths, cross-thread shared state, and coupling with the KV sync loop which increases tail latency and makes incremental refactors risky. Recent incidents showed elevated p95 generation latency during short bursts when the global aggregator contends with KV sync GC work.

Problem statement:
- Monolithic aggregator holds coarse locks during request admission and during KV prefix refresh causing head-of-line blocking for latency-sensitive calls.
- KV store sync is triggered synchronously from the aggregator in several hot paths; it causes CPU spikes and degraded throughput under load.
- The codebase depends on older async primitives and several internal crates are pinned to older minor versions (we observe contention patterns that newer runtime primitives can mitigate).

Goal:
Decompose the request aggregator into a lightweight admission/merge front-end and a separate compact, shard-aware KV sync coordinator. Reduce locking and cross-thread contention, update select runtime dependencies, and validate via bench and chaos tests. Target measurable improvements: >=10% throughput increase for steady-state generation at 128-token windows and >=15% reduction in p95 latency under bursty workloads while keeping cache hit rates +/-1% of baseline.

Scope / Proposed approach:
1) Decompose aggregator into two logical components:
   - Admission layer (request-merge, per-model queueing, early reject/backpressure decisions). This should not perform KV sync or GC work. Use lock-free queue where possible and replace global mutex with per-model sharded locks.
   - KV sync coordinator (background, shard-aware, rate-limited sync + compaction). Runs on dedicated worker pool, exposes async checkpoint API.
2) Introduce a compact delta-sync algorithm for KV prefixes: only sync recently mutated slots and avoid full-prefix scans on admission. Add soft-rate limits and exponential backoff on sync retries.
3) Replace older async primitives in the hot-paths (legacy Mutex + threadpool) with tokio::sync primitives and upgrade tokio minor version to leverage new parker improvements (see dependency plan below).
4) Add observability: detailed per-stage timing (admission.latency, merge.latency, kvsync.duration), contention metrics, and per-shard sync counters.
5) Migration strategy: feature-flagged rollout, canary on dedicated pools, automatic fallback to legacy aggregator on anomalous regressions.

Dependency upgrades (non-exhaustive):
- tokio: 1.25 -> 1.28 (gain improvements in task wake/parker).
- crossbeam: bump to latest release that includes wait-free queue fixes.
- bump small internal crates that expose KV index APIs to remove a couple of synchronous calls.
Note: upgrade plan includes smoke testing for all affected components in staging.

Acceptance criteria:
- Unit tests and integration tests updated and green.
- Bench harness (perf/continuous-batcher) shows >=10% throughput or >=15% p95 win in defined workloads (see perf PR).
- No cache hit-rate regressions >1% vs baseline across 24h soak in canary.
- All new metrics are emitted and wired into dashboards.
- Rollout plan validated: canary -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% with automatic rollback on error budget burn.

Migration / Rollout plan:
- Merge behind feature flag.
- Canary on a small set of dedicated pools (nightly low-traffic window).
- 24h soak and automated checks for latency, error rates, cache hit-rate, and GPU utilization.
- Gradual ramp with ops-runbook for manual rollback.

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: new background sync worker might lag and increase cold-prefix misses. Mitigation: conservative backoff defaults and aggressive warmup hooks when workload detected.
- Risk: dependency upgrades could surface unrelated regressions. Mitigation: pin non-critical services to legacy runtime until staged smoke tests pass and use canary gating.

Monitoring & Dashboards:
- runtime.batch.admission.latency.p95, runtime.batch.merge.latency.p95, runtime.kvsync.duration.p95, runtime.kvsync.queue.depth, runtime.kvsync.sync.errors.
- Add alert if p95 generation latency increases by >10% from baseline during canary.

Deliverables:
- RFC/Design doc linked in Confluence describing interfaces and migration (https://confluence.redwood.com/pages/RT-52614).
- Implementation PR with unit tests and benchmarks (see PR below).
- Perf dashboard snapshot comparing baseline vs canary.

Artifacts:
- Design doc: https://confluence.redwood.com/pages/RT-52614
- Perf harness: https://github.com/redwood-inference/perf/tree/main/continuous-aggregator-bench
- Implementation PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1489
comments: 2026-03-04 - Ava Patel: Created ticket after investigating a production incident (INC-2026-031). Attached preliminary flame graphs and contention traces. Recommended decomposition rather than incremental fixes.
2026-03-06 - Marcus Chen: Architecture sketch added to Confluence. Proposing per-model sharded queues and a small worker pool (2-4 threads) for KV sync. Will prototype lightweight admission first.
2026-03-08 - Priya Rao (SRE): Important to include conservative defaults behind a feature flag and automatic rollback when ops error budget triggers. Added runbook checklist in the design doc.

2026-03-09 - Marcus Chen: Opened implementation PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1489. Initial microbench shows 12% throughput improvement on synthetic steady workload (128 tokens), p95 down ~18% under bursty arrival pattern. Data attached in PR comments.
2026-03-11 - Code review: Geoff Li requested stronger invariants around shard ownership and added a test plan for cross-shard race scenarios. Addressed in PR iteration.

2026-03-12 - QA: Smoke tests in staging (8h soak) passed. Observed small increase in kvsync queue depth during first warmup period but steady-state metrics matched baseline. Preparing canary rollout documentation.
